root_idea.summary: The root has two principal semantic branches: the طَلْح tree and physical emaciation or exhaustion, with a figurative extension to badness or corruption.
root_idea.development: The lexical evidence keeps the tree branch distinct from the branch of wasting and fatigue; the latter also yields expressions for poor condition, weariness, and figurative badness.

qac_form_accounting.reason: The form is Quran-attested as a nominal lexical item and merits its own normalized dictionary headword.

senses.definition: A talh tree: a large, thorny tree of the acacia or mimosa-like ʿiḍāh kind.
senses.usage_conditions: In the Quranic occurrence, this interpretation identifies the word with the tree known as طَلْح; the collective noun has the singular طَلْحَة.
A lexicographical interpretation of the tree mentioned in 56:29; this identification is reported as disputed in the classical evidence.

senses.definition: The spadix or spathe of a palm tree, as a dialectal or letter-substitution variant of طَلْع.
senses.usage_conditions: This is another reported interpretation of the Quranic occurrence in 56:29, rather than the ordinary tree sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To suffer a belly complaint, or to be described as having such a complaint; especially said of camels affected after eating طَلْح.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The adjectival form is applied to camels. The evidence records a competing explanation that the condition denotes fatigue rather than digestive disorder.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To be, or to have, empty or void of food in the belly; also, the state of having the belly empty of food.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verbal use is said of a person, while the nominal description denotes the corresponding condition.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To become lean, emaciated, fatigued, or jaded; طَلِيحٌ describes one rendered lean or exhausted.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verb is especially used of a camel, including one exhausted by travel, disease, or exertion; طَلِيحٌ may be applied to camels and other animals. It can also describe a she-camel jaded by journeys.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To render someone or something lean or emaciated, or to fatigue it.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The direct object may be a camel or another being subjected to fatigue; the form also has the derived verbal noun تَطْلِيحٌ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To become bad, corrupt, or vicious.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative use, explicitly contrasted with becoming صالح; it is applied to a person.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To importune or press someone persistently until he becomes weary.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Especially said of pressing a debtor; the expression is figurative and has the verbal noun تَطْلِيحٌ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The remains of turbid water in a watering-trough or tank.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A nominal use referring to residual, muddied water.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A tick, especially a large tick.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The word is used for the parasitic insect; related expressions extend from this sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A keeper, manager, or good herder of camels or cattle.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An idiomatic expression based on the tick's attachment and persistence with its host.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who habitually pursues or follows women.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An idiomatic, figurative expression describing frequent pursuit.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A fatigued or weary herder or pastor; in the plural, herders or pastors.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This is a specialized pastoral use distinct from the insect sense and from the general adjective for an exhausted animal.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Enjoyment of a life of ease and plenty.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The form is specifically distinguished from the similarly written tree noun by its vocalization.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Land abounding in طَلْح trees.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An adjectival description of a place or tract of land.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The louse.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A fixed lexical expression.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A piece of paper.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The evidence labels this usage postclassical rather than an ordinary early Classical Arabic term.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Badness, corruptness, or viciousness.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative noun applied to a person and contrasted with صَلَاح.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Bad, corrupt, vicious, or without good.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An adjectival description of a person, explicitly contrasted with صَالِح.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Descriptive of camels feeding upon طِلَاح or طَلْح trees.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A relational or descriptive adjective used with camels; it does not introduce a separate tree species.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who acts wrongfully, unjustly, or injuriously with respect to property, camels, or cattle.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized participial description concerning wrongful treatment or dealings.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who breathes hard or emits a moaning sound while speaking.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reported lexical use in speech; the source notes a possible uncertainty in the related synonym's reading.

cautions: The single Quran occurrence at 56:29 has multiple reported lexical interpretations: the talh tree, banana trees, and طَلْع, the palm spadix or spathe. The contextual English rendering favors banana trees but does not resolve the classical disagreement.

The camel-related evidence records disagreement over whether طَلِحٌ denotes a belly complaint caused by eating طلح or fatigue and emaciation; both attested explanations are preserved separately in the Classical coverage. The hard-breathing use of مُطَلِّح is likewise reported with some uncertainty in the associated wording.
